planting.note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; this Mascarene palm needs frost-free conditions year-round.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun within a frost-free zone 10b-11 landscape. This Réunion Island relative of the bottle palm and spindle palm carries a gray trunk that is only gently swollen rather than sharply bottle- or spindle-shaped, tapering gradually up to a slim green crownshaft of arching pinnate fronds. It grows slowly and stays compact enough for tight courtyard or poolside plantings in tropical climates. Give it steady moisture while young, then moderate watering once established, and protect it from salt spray and any hint of frost.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets in spring or plant container stock into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Native to the mountains of northeastern Mexico, this species forms a rosette of broad, gray-green, yucca-like leaves much like Beschorneria yuccoides but is noticeably more cold-tolerant, making it a favorite of hardy-exotic gardeners pushing agave-relatives into cooler zones than typical for the genus. Mature rosettes send up an arching flower scape with coral-pink to red bracts and pendant greenish-yellow bells, after which that rosette declines while basal offsets carry the colony forward. Once established it tolerates considerable summer drought and prefers to stay on the dry side through winter.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring near a low shrub or trellis in part shade to full sun in gritty, well-drained soil.

directions: Plant in gritty, free-draining soil in part shade to full sun. A slender, wiry twiner from the dry woodlands and mallee country of southern Australia, it carries small bell-shaped flowers in dusky blue-mauve to greenish tones along its climbing stems, followed by oblong blue-purple berries with an edible, tart-sweet pulp. It is noticeably more drought-adapted than its woodland relative Billardiera scandens, making it well suited to scrambling through a dry native hedgerow or over a low fence where supplemental summer water is minimal.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into consistently moist, mineral-rich, serpentine-influenced seep soil that stays wet through spring.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, mineral-rich seep or bog-margin soil in part sun. Restricted to serpentine seeps and wet meadows of the Klamath-Siskiyou region of northern California and southern Oregon, this is the odd one out in a genus otherwise known for white flowers — its tall, slender spikes carry deep maroon-purple blooms instead. It grows from a bulb-like rhizome, flowering in late spring before going summer-dormant as its seep habitat dries. Best reserved for a dedicated bog bed or native-plant seep garden that mimics its mineral-soil, year-round-moisture habitat rather than a conventional border.
sources: USDA Forest Service Klamath-Siskiyou plant surveys

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical climates (zone 11-12) in full sun to light shade in deep, moist, well-drained forest soil.

directions: Plant in deep, moist, well-drained rainforest-type soil in full sun to light shade within humid equatorial climates only. This West and Central African forest tree is the close, bitter-fruited counterpart to the sweet bush mango (Irvingia gabonensis), sharing its general habit and leaf form but bearing smaller fruit with astringent, inedible pulp on a different fruiting schedule. Its real value is in the oil-rich kernel: dried and ground, it yields the thick, mucilaginous 'ogbono' used as a soup-thickening staple across Nigerian and Cameroonian cuisine, and it is grown commercially in West African agroforestry systems for that kernel trade rather than for fresh eating. Needs consistent rainfall or irrigation and does not tolerate drought, salinity, or any cold.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
